concepts.name: Real Number
concepts.meaning: A number placed on the usual number line.
concepts.formal: Real numbers include integers, fractions, and numbers such as $\sqrt{2}$ and $\pi$.

check.explanation: Real numbers lie on the ordinary number line.

concepts.linkedFormal: Real numbers include integers, fractions, and numbers such as $\sqrt{2}$ and $\pi$.

concepts.name: Integer
concepts.meaning: A whole number, including zero and negative whole numbers.
concepts.formal: Integers are $\ldots,-2,-1,0,1,2,\ldots$.

check.explanation: Integers have no fractional part.

concepts.linkedFormal: Integers are $\ldots,-2,-1,0,1,2,\ldots$.

concepts.name: Basic Algebra
concepts.meaning: Rules for working with numbers, letters, sums, and products.
concepts.formal: Use arithmetic, substitution, and equations, for example $a(b+c)=ab+ac$.

check.explanation: Divide both sides by 2.

concepts.linkedFormal: Use arithmetic, substitution, and equations, for example $a(b+c)=ab+ac$.

concepts.name: Set
concepts.meaning: A collection of objects.
concepts.formal: $x\in S$ means that $x$ belongs to the set $S$.

check.explanation: The symbol means membership.

concepts.linkedFormal: $x\in S$ means that $x$ belongs to the set $S$.

concepts.name: Function
concepts.meaning: A rule that assigns one output to each allowed input.
concepts.formal: A function $f$ sends an input $x$ to a single output $f(x)$.

check.explanation: Substitute 3 into the rule.

concepts.linkedFormal: A function $f$ sends an input $x$ to a single output $f(x)$.

concepts.name: Coordinate
concepts.meaning: A number specifying a location relative to a chosen reference.
concepts.formal: The coordinates $(x_1,x_2)$ locate a point using two chosen directions.
concepts.example: $(2,3)$ is two units across and three units up.

check.explanation: Count the entries.

concepts.linkedFormal: The coordinates $(x_1,x_2)$ locate a point using two chosen directions.

concepts.name: Complex Number Arithmetic
concepts.meaning: Arithmetic with numbers of the form $a+ib$, where $i^2=-1$.
concepts.formal: For real $a,b$, add and multiply $a+ib$ using ordinary algebra and $i^2=-1$.

check.explanation: This is the defining rule for i.

concepts.linkedFormal: For real $a,b$, add and multiply $a+ib$ using ordinary algebra and $i^2=-1$.

concepts.name: Derivative
concepts.meaning: The rate at which a function changes.
concepts.formal: The derivative $df/dx$ measures local change of the output with input $x$.

check.explanation: Use the school-level power rule.

concepts.linkedFormal: The derivative $df/dx$ measures local change of the output with input $x$.

concepts.name: Integral
concepts.meaning: A way to add continuously varying small contributions.
concepts.formal: $\int_a^b f(x)\,dx$ adds the contributions $f(x)\,dx$ between $a$ and $b$.

check.explanation: Evaluate x²/2 at the two endpoints.

concepts.linkedFormal: $\int_a^b f(x)\,dx$ adds the contributions $f(x)\,dx$ between $a$ and $b$.

concepts.name: Absolute Value
concepts.meaning: The nonnegative size of a number.
concepts.formal: For $z=a+ib$, its absolute value is $|z|=\sqrt{a^2+b^2}$.

check.explanation: Use the square root of 3²+4².

concepts.linkedFormal: For $z=a+ib$, its absolute value is $|z|=\sqrt{a^2+b^2}$.

concepts.name: Axiom
concepts.meaning: A starting rule accepted in a mathematical definition.
concepts.formal: An axiom states a rule assumed for the objects under discussion; other conclusions follow from those rules.

check.explanation: It supplies a starting point for deductions.

concepts.linkedFormal: An axiom states a rule assumed for the objects under discussion; other conclusions follow from those rules.

concepts.name: Field
concepts.meaning: A collection of numbers where addition, subtraction, multiplication, and division by nonzero numbers work.
concepts.formal: A field is a set with addition and multiplication, associative and commutative, with $0$, $1\ne0$, additive inverses, multiplicative inverses for nonzero elements, and $a(b+c)=ab+ac$.
concepts.example: $\mathbb R$ and $\mathbb C$ are fields; integers fail because $1/2$ is not an integer.

check.prompt: Why are integers not a field?
check.explanation: 2 has no integer multiplicative inverse.

concepts.linkedFormal: A field is a [[Set|set]] with [[Basic Algebra|addition]] and multiplication, [[Associativity|associative]] and [[Commutativity|commutative]], with $0$, $1\ne0$, additive inverses, multiplicative inverses for nonzero elements, and $a(b+c)=ab+ac$.

concepts.name: Scalar
concepts.meaning: A number used to scale an object.
concepts.formal: A scalar is an element of the field of numbers used for the vector space.

check.explanation: It is the multiplying number.

concepts.linkedFormal: A scalar is an element of the [[Field|field]] of numbers used for the [[Vector Space|vector space]].

concepts.name: Vector
concepts.meaning: An object that can be added to another of its kind and multiplied by a number.
concepts.formal: For a coordinate example, $v=(v_1,\ldots,v_n)$ has scalar entries; addition and scaling act entry by entry. Abstract vectors may instead be functions or state symbols with specified addition and scaling.

check.explanation: Add matching coordinates.

concepts.linkedFormal: For a [[Coordinate|coordinate]] example, $v=(v_1,\ldots,v_n)$ has [[Scalar|scalar]] entries; [[Basic Algebra|addition]] and scaling act entry by entry. Abstract vectors may instead be functions or [[Quantum State|state]] symbols with specified [[Basic Algebra|addition]] and scaling.

concepts.name: Closure
concepts.meaning: Combining allowed objects produces another allowed object.
concepts.formal: A set $V$ is closed under addition and scalar multiplication when $u+v\in V$ and $av\in V$ for all $u,v\in V$ and allowed scalars $a$.
concepts.example: Real coordinate pairs stay real coordinate pairs after addition.

check.explanation: The result must stay in the set.

concepts.linkedFormal: A [[Set|set]] $V$ is closed under [[Basic Algebra|addition]] and [[Scalar|scalar multiplication]] when $u+v\in V$ and $av\in V$ for all $u,v\in V$ and allowed [[Scalar|scalars]] $a$.

concepts.name: Zero Vector
concepts.meaning: The vector that leaves another vector unchanged when added.
concepts.formal: $v+0=v$ for every vector $v$.
concepts.example: In two coordinates the zero vector is $(0,0)$.

check.prompt: Which is the zero vector in two coordinates?
check.explanation: Both entries must be zero.

concepts.linkedFormal: $v+0=v$ for every [[Vector|vector]] $v$.

concepts.name: Additive Inverse
concepts.meaning: A vector that cancels another vector when added.
concepts.formal: For every vector $v$, its additive inverse $-v$ satisfies $v+(-v)=0$.

check.explanation: Reverse the sign of each coordinate.

concepts.linkedFormal: For every [[Vector|vector]] $v$, its additive inverse $-v$ satisfies $v+(-v)=0$.

concepts.name: Vector Space
concepts.meaning: A collection of vectors that obey consistent rules for addition and scaling.
concepts.formal: A vector space $V$ over a field $F$ is closed under addition and scalar multiplication. Addition is associative and commutative, has a zero vector and additive inverses; $a(u+v)=au+av$, $(a+b)v=av+bv$, $(ab)v=a(bv)$, and $1v=v$.
concepts.example: $\mathbb C^2$ with entrywise operations is a vector space. The set of positive real numbers is not: it lacks zero and negatives.

check.prompt: Which fails to be a vector space over the reals?
check.explanation: Check zero and additive inverses.

concepts.linkedFormal: A vector space $V$ over a [[Field|field]] $F$ is closed under [[Basic Algebra|addition]] and [[Scalar|scalar multiplication]]. [[Basic Algebra|Addition]] is [[Associativity|associative]] and [[Commutativity|commutative]], has a [[Zero Vector|zero vector]] and additive inverses; $a(u+v)=au+av$, $(a+b)v=av+bv$, $(ab)v=a(bv)$, and $1v=v$.

concepts.name: Linear Combination
concepts.meaning: A sum of vectors after multiplying each by a number.
concepts.formal: $a_1v_1+\cdots+a_nv_n$ is a linear combination with scalar coefficients $a_i$.

check.explanation: It uses only addition and scalar multiplication.

concepts.linkedFormal: $a_1v_1+\cdots+a_nv_n$ is a linear combination with [[Scalar|scalar]] coefficients $a_i$.

concepts.name: Linear Independence
concepts.meaning: No vector in the collection can be made from the others.
concepts.formal: $v_1,\ldots,v_n$ are linearly independent if $\sum_i a_iv_i=0$ implies every $a_i=0$.
concepts.example: $(1,0)$ and $(0,1)$ are independent; $(1,0)$ and $(2,0)$ are not.

options: No; one is twice the other
check.explanation: A nontrivial combination 2v₁−v₂ gives zero.

concepts.linkedFormal: $v_1,\ldots,v_n$ are linearly independent if $\sum_i a_iv_i=0$ implies every $a_i=0$.

concepts.name: Span
concepts.meaning: All vectors you can make from a given collection.
concepts.formal: The span of $v_1,\ldots,v_n$ is the set of all their linear combinations.
concepts.example: The span of $(1,0)$ is the horizontal line.

check.explanation: You can multiply by any allowed scalar.

concepts.linkedFormal: The span of $v_1,\ldots,v_n$ is the [[Set|set]] of all their linear combinations.

concepts.name: Basis
concepts.meaning: An independent collection from which every vector can be built.
concepts.formal: A basis is a linearly independent set spanning the vector space; in finite dimensions every vector has a unique expansion in it.
concepts.example: $e_1=(1,0)$ and $e_2=(0,1)$ form a basis of $\mathbb R^2$.

options: Be independent and span the space
check.explanation: Both conditions are required.

concepts.linkedFormal: A basis is a linearly independent [[Set|set]] spanning the [[Vector Space|vector space]]; in finite dimensions every [[Vector|vector]] has a unique expansion in it.

concepts.name: Dimension
concepts.meaning: The number of independent directions in a space.
concepts.formal: The dimension of a finite-dimensional vector space is the number of vectors in any basis.

check.prompt: How many basis vectors does $\mathbb C^2$ need?
check.explanation: Dimension counts vectors over the chosen field.

concepts.linkedFormal: The dimension of a finite-dimensional [[Vector Space|vector space]] is the [[Real Number|number]] of [[Vector|vectors]] in any [[Basis|basis]].

concepts.name: Complex Conjugate
concepts.meaning: A complex number with the sign of its imaginary part reversed.
concepts.formal: If $z=a+ib$, then $z^*=a-ib$; $(zw)^*=z^*w^*$.

check.explanation: Only the imaginary part changes sign.

concepts.linkedFormal: If $z=a+ib$, then $z^*=a-ib$; $(zw)^*=z^*w^*$.

concepts.name: Inner Product
concepts.meaning: A rule that pairs two vectors and returns a number measuring their overlap.
concepts.formal: Using the physics convention, $\langle u|av+bw\rangle=a\langle u|v\rangle+b\langle u|w\rangle$, $\langle u|v\rangle=\langle v|u\rangle^*$, and $\langle v|v\rangle\ge0$, with equality only for $v=0$. In $\mathbb C^n$, $\langle u|v\rangle=\sum_i u_i^*v_i$.

check.prompt: Which entry gets conjugated in $\langle u|v\rangle$?
check.explanation: The physics convention is conjugate-linear in the first slot.

concepts.linkedFormal: Using the physics convention, $\langle u|av+bw\rangle=a\langle u|v\rangle+b\langle u|w\rangle$, $\langle u|v\rangle=\langle v|u\rangle^*$, and $\langle v|v\rangle\ge0$, with equality only for $v=0$. In $\mathbb C^n$, $\langle u|v\rangle=\sum_i u_i^*v_i$.

concepts.name: Conjugate Symmetry
concepts.meaning: Swapping the two vectors conjugates their overlap.
concepts.formal: $\langle u|v\rangle=\langle v|u\rangle^*$.

check.explanation: Conjugate the scalar product.

concepts.linkedFormal: $\langle u|v\rangle=\langle v|u\rangle^*$.

concepts.name: Norm
concepts.meaning: The length of a vector.
concepts.formal: The norm induced by an inner product is $\|v\|=\sqrt{\langle v|v\rangle}$.

check.explanation: Take the square root of the self-inner-product.

concepts.linkedFormal: The norm induced by an [[Inner Product|inner product]] is $\|v\|=\sqrt{\langle v|v\rangle}$.

concepts.name: Orthogonality
concepts.meaning: Two vectors have zero overlap.
concepts.formal: $u$ and $v$ are orthogonal when $\langle u|v\rangle=0$.

check.prompt: Orthogonal vectors have which inner product?
check.explanation: Zero overlap defines orthogonality.

concepts.linkedFormal: $u$ and $v$ are orthogonal when $\langle u|v\rangle=0$.

concepts.name: Normalization
concepts.meaning: Scaling a nonzero vector so its length is one.
concepts.formal: For nonzero $v$, the normalized vector is $v/\|v\|$.

check.explanation: Divide the vector by its norm.

concepts.linkedFormal: For nonzero $v$, the normalized [[Vector|vector]] is $v/\|v\|$.

concepts.name: Orthonormal Basis
concepts.meaning: A basis of unit-length vectors that have zero overlap with each other.
concepts.formal: $\langle e_i|e_j\rangle=\delta_{ij}$, where the number $\delta_{ij}$ is 1 if $i=j$ and 0 otherwise. These vectors form a basis.

check.explanation: Different basis vectors are orthogonal.

concepts.linkedFormal: $\langle e_i|e_j\rangle=\delta_{ij}$, where the [[Real Number|number]] $\delta_{ij}$ is 1 if $i=j$ and 0 otherwise. These [[Vector|vectors]] form a [[Basis|basis]].

concepts.name: Sequence
concepts.meaning: An ordered list indexed by counting numbers.
concepts.formal: A sequence is a function assigning an object $v_n$ to each positive integer $n$.

check.explanation: The index counts entries.

concepts.linkedFormal: A sequence is a [[Function|function]] assigning an object $v_n$ to each positive [[Integer|integer]] $n$.

concepts.name: Limit
concepts.meaning: A value that a sequence approaches arbitrarily closely.
concepts.formal: $x_n\to L$ means for every real $\epsilon>0$, some integer $N$ has $|x_n-L|<\epsilon$ for all $n>N$.

check.prompt: What is the limit of $1/n$ as $n$ grows?
check.explanation: The entries approach zero without needing to reach it.

concepts.linkedFormal: $x_n\to L$ means for every real $\epsilon>0$, some [[Integer|integer]] $N$ has $|x_n-L|<\epsilon$ for all $n>N$.

concepts.name: Convergence
concepts.meaning: The terms of a sequence approach a vector in distance.
concepts.formal: A sequence $v_n$ converges in norm to $v$ if $\|v_n-v\|\to0$.

check.explanation: Measure distance from the candidate limit.

concepts.linkedFormal: A [[Sequence|sequence]] $v_n$ converges in [[Norm|norm]] to $v$ if $\|v_n-v\|\to0$.

concepts.name: Cauchy Sequence
concepts.meaning: A sequence whose later terms get arbitrarily close to each other.
concepts.formal: For every $\epsilon>0$, there is $N$ with $\|v_n-v_m\|<\epsilon$ whenever $n,m>N$.
concepts.example: The partial sums of $\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}2^{-k}$ are Cauchy.

options: Only the first and last term
check.explanation: It does not assume a limit is already in the space.

concepts.linkedFormal: For every $\epsilon>0$, there is $N$ with $\|v_n-v_m\|<\epsilon$ whenever $n,m>N$.

concepts.name: Complete Space
concepts.meaning: A space with no missing limits of Cauchy sequences.
concepts.formal: A normed space is complete when every Cauchy sequence in it converges to an element of the same space.
concepts.example: Rational numbers are incomplete: rational approximations can approach $\sqrt2$, which is not rational.

check.explanation: The location of the limit matters.

concepts.linkedFormal: A [[Normed Space|normed space]] is complete when every [[Cauchy Sequence|Cauchy sequence]] in it converges to an element of the same [[Mathematical Space|space]].

concepts.name: Hilbert Space
concepts.meaning: A vector space with an overlap rule and no missing limits measured by that rule.
concepts.formal: A Hilbert space is an inner-product vector space complete in the induced norm $\|v\|=\sqrt{\langle v|v\rangle}$.
concepts.example: $\mathbb C^2$ with its usual inner product is a Hilbert space.

check.prompt: What extra condition makes an inner-product space Hilbert?
check.explanation: Every Cauchy sequence must converge inside it.

concepts.linkedFormal: A Hilbert space is an [[Inner Product|inner-product]] [[Vector Space|vector space]] complete in the induced [[Norm|norm]] $\|v\|=\sqrt{\langle v|v\rangle}$.

concepts.name: Ket
concepts.meaning: A notation for a quantum state vector.
concepts.formal: $|\psi\rangle$ denotes a vector in the Hilbert space. In a chosen basis it can be represented as a column of coefficients.

check.explanation: The bracket is notation for a state vector.

concepts.linkedFormal: $|\psi\rangle$ denotes a [[Vector|vector]] in the [[Hilbert Space|Hilbert space]]. In a chosen [[Basis|basis]] it can be represented as a column of coefficients.

concepts.name: Bra
concepts.meaning: The rule associated with a ket that takes another ket and returns their overlap.
concepts.formal: The bra $\langle\psi|$ maps $|\phi\rangle$ to $\langle\psi|\phi\rangle$. For coordinates $\begin{pmatrix}a\\b\end{pmatrix}$, its row is $(a^*,b^*)$.

check.explanation: Transpose and conjugate the coordinates.

concepts.linkedFormal: The bra $\langle\psi|$ maps $|\phi\rangle$ to $\langle\psi|\phi\rangle$. For [[Coordinate|coordinates]] $\begin{pmatrix}a\\b\end{pmatrix}$, its row is $(a^*,b^*)$.

concepts.name: Linear Operator
concepts.meaning: A rule taking vectors to vectors while respecting addition and scaling.
concepts.formal: $A(a|u\rangle+b|v\rangle)=aA|u\rangle+bA|v\rangle$. The input vectors must belong to the operator domain.
concepts.example: $A(x,y)=(2x,3y)$ is linear. $A(x)=x^2$ is not linear over real numbers.

check.explanation: Check addition and scalar multiplication.

concepts.linkedFormal: $A(a|u\rangle+b|v\rangle)=aA|u\rangle+bA|v\rangle$. The input [[Vector|vectors]] must belong to the [[Operator Domain|operator domain]].

concepts.name: Operator Domain
concepts.meaning: The set of vectors on which an operator is defined.
concepts.formal: $D(A)$ is the set of allowed inputs of $A$. For a derivative on square-integrable functions, extra differentiability and boundary conditions are required.
concepts.example: Not every square-integrable function has a square-integrable derivative.

check.prompt: Is a derivative defined on every square-integrable function?
check.explanation: Some such functions are not differentiable.

concepts.linkedFormal: $D(A)$ is the [[Set|set]] of allowed inputs of $A$. For a [[Derivative|derivative]] on square-integrable functions, extra [[Derivative|differentiability]] and boundary conditions are required.

concepts.name: Operator Product
concepts.meaning: Apply one operator and then another.
concepts.formal: $(AB)|v\rangle=A(B|v\rangle)$ wherever both applications are defined. The rightmost operator acts first.

check.explanation: Read composition from right to left.

concepts.linkedFormal: $(AB)|v\rangle=A(B|v\rangle)$ wherever both applications are defined. The rightmost [[Linear Operator|operator]] acts first.

concepts.name: Identity Operator
concepts.meaning: The operator that leaves every vector unchanged.
concepts.formal: $I|v\rangle=|v\rangle$.
concepts.example: Its two-dimensional matrix has diagonal entries 1 and off-diagonal entries 0.

check.explanation: Identity means no change.

concepts.linkedFormal: $I|v\rangle=|v\rangle$.

concepts.name: Hermitian Adjoint
concepts.meaning: The operator obtained by moving an operation across an inner product.
concepts.formal: $\langle u|Av\rangle=\langle A^\dagger u|v\rangle$ for allowed vectors. For matrices, $(A^\dagger)_{ij}=A_{ji}^*$.

check.prompt: How do you find a matrix adjoint?
check.explanation: Both operations are necessary.

concepts.linkedFormal: $\langle u|Av\rangle=\langle A^\dagger u|v\rangle$ for allowed [[Vector|vectors]]. For matrices, $(A^\dagger)_{ij}=A_{ji}^*$.

concepts.name: Hermitian Operator
concepts.meaning: An operator equal to its adjoint in the setting under consideration.
concepts.formal: In finite dimensions, Hermitian means $A=A^\dagger$, equivalently $\langle u|Av\rangle=\langle Au|v\rangle$. For unbounded operators, distinguish this symmetry identity from self-adjointness, which also requires equality of domains.

check.explanation: Match the matrix to its conjugate transpose.

concepts.linkedFormal: In finite dimensions, Hermitian means $A=A^\dagger$, equivalently $\langle u|Av\rangle=\langle Au|v\rangle$. For [[Operator Domain|unbounded]] operators, distinguish this [[Symmetric Operator|symmetry identity]] from [[Self-adjoint Operator|self-adjointness]], which also requires equality of domains.

concepts.name: Self-adjoint Operator
concepts.meaning: An operator matching its adjoint in both action and allowed inputs.
concepts.formal: $A=A^\dagger$ and $D(A)=D(A^\dagger)$. In finite dimensions this is the same as being Hermitian.
concepts.example: The momentum derivative requires a suitable domain and boundary conditions to be self-adjoint.

check.prompt: For an unbounded self-adjoint operator, domains must…
check.explanation: Matching the formula alone is insufficient.

concepts.linkedFormal: $A=A^\dagger$ and $D(A)=D(A^\dagger)$. In finite dimensions this is the same as being [[Hermitian Operator|Hermitian]].

concepts.name: Commutator
concepts.meaning: The difference between applying two operators in opposite orders.
concepts.formal: $[A,B]=AB-BA$. Commuting operators satisfy $[A,B]=0$. The product rule is $[A,BC]=[A,B]C+B[A,C]$.
concepts.example: $[x,p]=i\hbar I$ in the canonical position–momentum setting.

check.explanation: It subtracts the reversed product.

concepts.linkedFormal: $[A,B]=AB-BA$. Commuting operators satisfy $[A,B]=0$. The product rule is $[A,BC]=[A,B]C+B[A,C]$.

concepts.name: Anticommutator
concepts.meaning: The sum of two operator products in opposite orders.

check.explanation: Add the two identical products.

concepts.name: Function of an Operator
concepts.meaning: A function evaluated with an operator in place of its input.
concepts.formal: For a polynomial, $f(A)=\sum_{n=0}^{N}c_nA^n$ with $A^0=I$. A power series requires convergence; more general definitions need a suitable spectral construction.

check.explanation: The constant term multiplies the identity.

concepts.linkedFormal: For a [[Polynomial|polynomial]], $f(A)=\sum_{n=0}^{N}c_nA^n$ with $A^0=I$. A power series requires [[Convergence|convergence]]; more general definitions need a suitable spectral construction.

concepts.name: Eigenvector
concepts.meaning: A nonzero vector whose direction stays the same under an operator.
concepts.formal: $A|v\rangle=\lambda|v\rangle$ with $|v\rangle\ne0$ makes $|v\rangle$ an eigenvector.

check.prompt: Can the zero vector be an eigenvector?
check.explanation: Nonzero is part of the definition.

concepts.linkedFormal: $A|v\rangle=\lambda|v\rangle$ with $|v\rangle\ne0$ makes $|v\rangle$ an eigenvector.

concepts.name: Eigenvalue
concepts.meaning: The factor by which an operator scales an eigenvector.
concepts.formal: If $A|v\rangle=\lambda|v\rangle$ for nonzero $|v\rangle$, then $\lambda$ is its eigenvalue.

check.explanation: Read the multiplying scalar.

concepts.linkedFormal: If $A|v\rangle=\lambda|v\rangle$ for nonzero $|v\rangle$, then $\lambda$ is its eigenvalue.

concepts.name: Degeneracy
concepts.meaning: Several independent eigenvectors share the same eigenvalue.
concepts.formal: An eigenvalue is degenerate if its eigenspace, the set of its eigenvectors together with zero, has dimension greater than 1.
concepts.example: $A=2I$ on $\mathbb C^2$ has eigenvalue 2 with degeneracy 2.

check.prompt: For $2I$ in two dimensions, the degeneracy of 2 is…
check.explanation: There are two independent eigenvectors.

concepts.linkedFormal: An [[Eigenvalue|eigenvalue]] is degenerate if its [[Eigenspace|eigenspace]], the [[Set|set]] of its [[Eigenvector|eigenvectors]] together with zero, has [[Dimension|dimension]] greater than 1.

concepts.name: Simultaneous Eigenvectors
concepts.meaning: Vectors that are eigenvectors of both operators.
concepts.formal: Finite-dimensional commuting Hermitian operators admit a common orthonormal eigenbasis. A nondegenerate eigenvector of $A$ is also an eigenvector of $B$; within a degenerate eigenspace choose a basis diagonalizing $B$. Commutation alone does not give this result for arbitrary defective operators.
concepts.example: Two diagonal matrices share the coordinate basis.

check.prompt: With degeneracy, does every eigenvector of A automatically diagonalize B?
options: No; choose a common basis within each eigenspace
check.explanation: B may mix vectors inside a degenerate eigenspace.

concepts.linkedFormal: [[Dimension|Finite-dimensional]] [[Commutator|commuting]] [[Hermitian Operator|Hermitian]] operators admit a common [[Orthonormal Basis|orthonormal eigenbasis]]. A nondegenerate [[Eigenvector|eigenvector]] of $A$ is also an [[Eigenvector|eigenvector]] of $B$; within a [[Degeneracy|degenerate]] [[Eigenspace|eigenspace]] choose a [[Basis|basis]] diagonalizing $B$. Commutation alone does not give this result for arbitrary defective operators.

concepts.name: Projection Operator
concepts.meaning: An operator that keeps a selected component of a vector.
concepts.formal: For normalized $|n\rangle$, $P_n=|n\rangle\langle n|$ and $P_n^2=P_n=P_n^\dagger$.

check.explanation: It takes an overlap and rebuilds that direction.

concepts.linkedFormal: For [[Normalization|normalized]] $|n\rangle$, $P_n=|n\rangle\langle n|$ and $P_n^2=P_n=P_n^\dagger$.

concepts.name: Completeness Relation
concepts.meaning: Adding all basis-component projections reconstructs every vector.
concepts.formal: For a complete orthonormal basis, $\sum_n|n\rangle\langle n|=I$ and $|\psi\rangle=\sum_n|n\rangle\langle n|\psi\rangle$. Infinite sums converge in the Hilbert-space norm.

check.prompt: The sum of all orthonormal basis projections equals…
check.explanation: All components together reconstruct the state.

concepts.linkedFormal: For a complete [[Orthonormal Basis|orthonormal basis]], $\sum_n|n\rangle\langle n|=I$ and $|\psi\rangle=\sum_n|n\rangle\langle n|\psi\rangle$. Infinite sums converge in the Hilbert-[[Mathematical Space|space]] [[Norm|norm]].

concepts.name: Spectral Theorem
concepts.meaning: A finite Hermitian matrix has a complete orthonormal set of eigenvectors.
concepts.formal: For an $n\times n$ Hermitian matrix, there is an orthonormal eigenbasis with real eigenvalues and $A=\sum_j\lambda_j|j\rangle\langle j|$. In infinite dimensions a self-adjoint operator has a spectral measure; normalizable eigenvectors need not form a discrete basis.

check.prompt: Does every infinite-dimensional observable have a discrete normalizable eigenbasis?
options: No; a continuous spectrum may occur
Only if its eigenvalues are real
check.explanation: Position is a standard continuous-spectrum example.

concepts.linkedFormal: For an $n\times n$ [[Hermitian Operator|Hermitian matrix]], there is an [[Orthonormal Basis|orthonormal eigenbasis]] with real [[Eigenvalue|eigenvalues]] and $A=\sum_j\lambda_j|j\rangle\langle j|$. In infinite dimensions a [[Self-adjoint Operator|self-adjoint operator]] has a spectral measure; [[Normalization|normalizable]] [[Eigenvector|eigenvectors]] need not form a discrete [[Basis|basis]].

concepts.name: Matrix
concepts.meaning: A rectangular array of numbers.
concepts.formal: A matrix $A$ has entries $A_{ij}$, with row $i$ and column $j$. Products satisfy $(AB)_{ij}=\sum_k A_{ik}B_{kj}$.

check.prompt: What does the second index of $A_{ij}$ specify?
check.explanation: The convention is row first, column second.

concepts.linkedFormal: A matrix $A$ has entries $A_{ij}$, with row $i$ and column $j$. Products satisfy $(AB)_{ij}=\sum_k A_{ik}B_{kj}$.

concepts.name: Matrix Representation
concepts.meaning: Numbers describing a state or operator in a chosen basis.
concepts.formal: State coordinates are $c_i=\langle i|\psi\rangle$. Operator entries are $A_{ij}=\langle i|A|j\rangle$, so column $j$ contains the coordinates of $A|j\rangle$.

check.prompt: Where do the coefficients of $A|1\rangle$ go?
check.explanation: The input basis index labels the column.

concepts.linkedFormal: [[Quantum State|State]] [[Coordinate|coordinates]] are $c_i=\langle i|\psi\rangle$. [[Linear Operator|Operator]] entries are $A_{ij}=\langle i|A|j\rangle$, so column $j$ contains the [[Coordinate|coordinates]] of $A|j\rangle$.

concepts.name: Unitary Operator
concepts.meaning: An invertible operator that preserves overlaps and lengths.
concepts.formal: $U^\dagger U=UU^\dagger=I$; hence $U^{-1}=U^\dagger$ and $\langle Uu|Uv\rangle=\langle u|v\rangle$.
concepts.example: A real rotation matrix is unitary.

check.prompt: For a unitary U, its inverse is…
check.explanation: Its adjoint reverses the transformation.

concepts.linkedFormal: $U^\dagger U=UU^\dagger=I$; hence $U^{-1}=U^\dagger$ and $\langle Uu|Uv\rangle=\langle u|v\rangle$.

concepts.name: Change of Basis
concepts.meaning: Describe the same object using different reference vectors.
concepts.formal: If $|e_j\rangle=\sum_i|i\rangle U_{ij}$, with columns the new orthonormal basis in old coordinates, then $c_{new}=U^\dagger c_{old}$ and $A_{new}=U^\dagger A_{old}U$.
concepts.example: Taking new basis vectors to be eigenvectors produces a diagonal operator matrix.

check.prompt: When U has new basis vectors as columns, the new matrix is…
check.explanation: Convert new coordinates to old, act, then convert back.

concepts.linkedFormal: If $|e_j\rangle=\sum_i|i\rangle U_{ij}$, with columns the new [[Orthonormal Basis|orthonormal basis]] in old [[Coordinate|coordinates]], then $c_{new}=U^\dagger c_{old}$ and $A_{new}=U^\dagger A_{old}U$.

concepts.name: Determinant
concepts.meaning: A number that detects whether a square matrix can be inverted.
concepts.formal: For $A=\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\c&d\end{pmatrix}$, $\det A=ad-bc$. More generally, it is the signed sum over all permutations of column choices. $\det A=0$ exactly when a finite square matrix has a nonzero vector sent to zero.

check.explanation: Multiply the diagonal entries and subtract the other product.

concepts.linkedFormal: For $A=\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\c&d\end{pmatrix}$, $\det A=ad-bc$. More generally, it is the signed sum over all permutations of column choices. $\det A=0$ exactly when a finite square [[Matrix|matrix]] has a nonzero [[Vector|vector]] sent to zero.

concepts.name: Secular Equation
concepts.meaning: The equation whose roots are matrix eigenvalues.
concepts.formal: $A v=\lambda v$ with $v\ne0$ requires $\det(A-\lambda I)=0$.

check.explanation: Move the eigenvalue term to the left.

concepts.linkedFormal: $A v=\lambda v$ with $v\ne0$ requires $\det(A-\lambda I)=0$.

concepts.name: Trace
concepts.meaning: The sum of a square matrix’s diagonal entries.
concepts.formal: $\operatorname{tr}A=\sum_i A_{ii}$. For finite square matrices, $\operatorname{tr}(AB)=\operatorname{tr}(BA)$, and the trace equals the sum of eigenvalues counted with multiplicity.

check.explanation: Add only the diagonal entries.

concepts.linkedFormal: $\operatorname{tr}A=\sum_i A_{ii}$. For finite square matrices, $\operatorname{tr}(AB)=\operatorname{tr}(BA)$, and the trace equals the sum of [[Eigenvalue|eigenvalues]] counted with [[Multiplicity|multiplicity]].

concepts.name: Exponential Function
concepts.meaning: A function whose rate of change equals itself.
concepts.formal: $d(e^x)/dx=e^x$, $e^{a+b}=e^ae^b$, and $e^{i\theta}=\cos\theta+i\sin\theta$.

check.explanation: It lies on the unit circle.

concepts.linkedFormal: $d(e^x)/dx=e^x$, $e^{a+b}=e^ae^b$, and $e^{i\theta}=\cos\theta+i\sin\theta$.

concepts.name: Square-Integrable Function
concepts.meaning: A function whose squared size has a finite integral.
concepts.formal: $f$ is square-integrable if $\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}|f(x)|^2dx<\infty$. Functions differing only on a set of zero length are identified. The resulting $L^2$ space is complete with $\langle f|g\rangle=\int f^*(x)g(x)dx$.
concepts.example: $e^{-|x|}$ is square-integrable; the constant function 1 on the whole line is not.

check.explanation: Integrate the squared magnitude, not the function itself.

concepts.linkedFormal: $f$ is square-integrable if $\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}|f(x)|^2dx<\infty$. Functions differing only on a [[Set|set]] of zero length are identified. The resulting $L^2$ [[Mathematical Space|space]] is complete with $\langle f|g\rangle=\int f^*(x)g(x)dx$.

concepts.name: Probability Density
concepts.meaning: A nonnegative function whose integral over an interval gives probability.
concepts.formal: $\rho(x)\ge0$, $\int\rho(x)dx=1$, and the probability in $[a,b]$ is $\int_a^b\rho(x)dx$. Density at a point is not itself an interval probability.
concepts.example: If $\rho(x)=1$ on $[0,1]$, the probability in $[0,1/4]$ is $1/4$.

options: The integral of density over it
check.explanation: Accumulate the density across the interval.

concepts.linkedFormal: $\rho(x)\ge0$, $\int\rho(x)dx=1$, and the [[Probability|probability]] in $[a,b]$ is $\int_a^b\rho(x)dx$. Density at a point is not itself an interval [[Probability|probability]].

concepts.name: Wave Function
concepts.meaning: The coefficients of a state expressed using a continuous coordinate.
concepts.formal: For a normalized state, $\psi(x)=\langle x|\psi\rangle$ and $|\psi(x)|^2$ is its position probability density. The overall phase does not change that density.
concepts.example: $\psi(x)=\sqrt a\,e^{-a|x|}$ with $a>0$ is normalized on the line.

check.explanation: Complex amplitudes need their absolute-value squared.

concepts.linkedFormal: For a [[Normalization|normalized]] [[Quantum State|state]], $\psi(x)=\langle x|\psi\rangle$ and $|\psi(x)|^2$ is its position [[Probability Density|probability density]]. The [[Phase|overall phase]] does not change that density.

concepts.name: Distribution
concepts.meaning: An object defined by how it acts on smooth functions rather than by pointwise values.
concepts.formal: A distribution is a linear, continuous rule on smooth test functions with compact support. The delta distribution acts as $\delta[f]=f(0)$. Compact support means the function vanishes outside some finite interval; continuity means small test-function changes give small output changes in this setting.
concepts.example: $\delta[x^2+1]=1$ when evaluated locally with a suitable test function.

check.explanation: This lets us define delta without pretending it is an ordinary function.

concepts.linkedFormal: A distribution is a linear, [[Continuity|continuous]] rule on [[Test Function|smooth test functions]] with [[Compact Support|compact support]]. The delta distribution acts as $\delta[f]=f(0)$. [[Compact Support|Compact support]] means the [[Function|function]] vanishes outside some finite interval; [[Continuity|continuity]] means small test-[[Function|function]] changes give small output changes in this setting.

concepts.name: Delta Function
concepts.meaning: An idealized point selector inside an integral.
concepts.formal: The Dirac delta is a distribution defined by $\int\delta(x-a)f(x)dx=f(a)$ for suitable smooth test functions. It is not an ordinary finite-valued function.

check.explanation: The delta selects the value at x=2.

concepts.linkedFormal: The Dirac delta is a [[Distribution|distribution]] defined by $\int\delta(x-a)f(x)dx=f(a)$ for suitable [[Test Function|smooth test functions]]. It is not an ordinary finite-valued [[Function|function]].

concepts.name: Continuous Basis
concepts.meaning: A continuously labelled family of generalized state symbols.
concepts.formal: Position states obey $\langle x|x\prime\rangle=\delta(x-x\prime)$ and $\int|x\rangle\langle x|dx=I$; momentum states obey the corresponding $p$ relations. These are generalized states, not normalizable vectors of $L^2$.
concepts.example: A physical wavepacket can be expanded as $|\psi\rangle=\int\psi(x)|x\rangle dx$.

check.prompt: Are exact position kets normalizable L² vectors?
check.explanation: Their overlap uses a distribution, not a finite norm.

concepts.linkedFormal: Position states obey $\langle x|x\prime\rangle=\delta(x-x\prime)$ and $\int|x\rangle\langle x|dx=I$; momentum states obey the corresponding $p$ relations. These are [[Generalized State|generalized states]], not [[Normalization|normalizable]] [[Vector|vectors]] of $L^2$.

concepts.name: Position Representation
concepts.meaning: Describe a quantum state using position as the input variable.
concepts.formal: $\psi(x)=\langle x|\psi\rangle$. For a normalized state, $\int|\psi(x)|^2dx=1$.
concepts.example: A localized packet has a density concentrated in a small position interval.

check.explanation: Project the ket onto the position bra.

concepts.linkedFormal: $\psi(x)=\langle x|\psi\rangle$. For a [[Normalization|normalized]] [[Quantum State|state]], $\int|\psi(x)|^2dx=1$.

concepts.name: Momentum Representation
concepts.meaning: Describe a quantum state using momentum as the input variable.
concepts.formal: $\phi(p)=\langle p|\psi\rangle$; $|\phi(p)|^2dp$ is the probability in a small momentum interval.
concepts.example: A narrow momentum density describes a state with nearly definite momentum.

check.explanation: Use the momentum bra.

concepts.linkedFormal: $\phi(p)=\langle p|\psi\rangle$; $|\phi(p)|^2dp$ is the [[Probability|probability]] in a small momentum interval.

concepts.name: Planck Constant
concepts.meaning: The constant setting the size of quantum effects.
concepts.formal: $\hbar=h/(2\pi)$ is the reduced Planck constant. It has units of action, energy multiplied by time.

check.prompt: How are h and ℏ related?
check.explanation: ℏ is the reduced constant.

concepts.linkedFormal: $\hbar=h/(2\pi)$ is the reduced Planck constant. It has units of action, energy multiplied by time.

concepts.name: Fourier Transform
concepts.meaning: A change from a function’s position description to its momentum description.
concepts.formal: $\phi(p)=\frac1{\sqrt{2\pi\hbar}}\int e^{-ipx/\hbar}\psi(x)dx$ and $\psi(x)=\frac1{\sqrt{2\pi\hbar}}\int e^{ipx/\hbar}\phi(p)dp$. With this convention it preserves the norm; integrals are understood in the $L^2$ sense when needed.
concepts.example: A sharply localized position packet needs a broad spread of momentum components.

check.explanation: Our forward convention uses the negative imaginary phase.

concepts.linkedFormal: $\phi(p)=\frac1{\sqrt{2\pi\hbar}}\int e^{-ipx/\hbar}\psi(x)dx$ and $\psi(x)=\frac1{\sqrt{2\pi\hbar}}\int e^{ipx/\hbar}\phi(p)dp$. With this convention it preserves the [[Norm|norm]]; integrals are understood in the $L^2$ sense when needed.

concepts.name: Position Operator
concepts.meaning: The operator that multiplies a position wave function by its coordinate.
concepts.formal: $(\hat x\psi)(x)=x\psi(x)$ on the domain with $x\psi\in L^2$.

check.prompt: In position space, x̂ acts by…
check.explanation: The coordinate is the position eigenvalue.

concepts.linkedFormal: $(\hat x\psi)(x)=x\psi(x)$ on the domain with $x\psi\in L^2$.

concepts.name: Momentum Operator
concepts.meaning: The operator that differentiates a position wave function with a quantum scale factor.
concepts.formal: $(\hat p\psi)(x)=-i\hbar\,d\psi/dx$ on a suitable domain. A plane wave $e^{ipx/\hbar}$ satisfies $\hat p e^{ipx/\hbar}=p e^{ipx/\hbar}$.

check.prompt: In position space, p̂ acts as…
check.explanation: Differentiate and multiply by −iℏ.

concepts.linkedFormal: $(\hat p\psi)(x)=-i\hbar\,d\psi/dx$ on a suitable domain. A plane wave $e^{ipx/\hbar}$ satisfies $\hat p e^{ipx/\hbar}=p e^{ipx/\hbar}$.

concepts.name: Integration by Parts
concepts.meaning: Move a derivative from one factor to the other inside an integral.
concepts.formal: $\int_a^b u(x)v\prime(x)dx=[uv]_a^b-\int_a^b u\prime(x)v(x)dx$.
concepts.example: Boundary terms vanish for suitably decaying functions on the whole line.

options: A boundary term and an integral with the derivative moved
check.explanation: Keep the boundary contribution until conditions remove it.

concepts.linkedFormal: $\int_a^b u(x)v\prime(x)dx=[uv]_a^b-\int_a^b u\prime(x)v(x)dx$.

concepts.name: Boundary Condition
concepts.meaning: A restriction on a function at the edge of its allowed region.
concepts.formal: Boundary conditions specify endpoint behavior, such as vanishing or periodic values. They help select the operator domain and justify removal of boundary terms.
concepts.example: Smooth decaying wave functions have zero boundary products at infinity.

check.prompt: When can a boundary term be dropped?
options: When the imposed boundary behavior makes it zero
check.explanation: State the boundary assumption explicitly.

concepts.linkedFormal: Boundary conditions specify endpoint behavior, such as vanishing or periodic values. They help select the [[Operator Domain|operator domain]] and justify removal of boundary terms.

concepts.name: Observable
concepts.meaning: A measurable physical quantity represented by an appropriate operator.
concepts.formal: Quantum observables are represented by self-adjoint operators, with measurement outcomes described by their spectra. In finite dimensions these are Hermitian matrices and their eigenvalues.

check.explanation: This ensures real possible outcomes.

concepts.linkedFormal: Quantum observables are represented by [[Self-adjoint Operator|self-adjoint]] operators, with measurement outcomes described by their [[Spectrum|spectra]]. In finite dimensions these are [[Hermitian Operator|Hermitian]] matrices and their [[Eigenvalue|eigenvalues]].

concepts.name: Expectation Value
concepts.meaning: The average predicted measurement result over many identical preparations.
concepts.formal: For a normalized state, $\langle A\rangle=\langle\psi|A|\psi\rangle$. For an unnormalized vector divide by $\langle\psi|\psi\rangle$.

check.prompt: For equal probabilities of 2 and 3, the expectation is…
check.explanation: Average the outcomes with their probabilities.

concepts.linkedFormal: For a [[Normalization|normalized]] [[Quantum State|state]], $\langle A\rangle=\langle\psi|A|\psi\rangle$. For an unnormalized [[Vector|vector]] divide by $\langle\psi|\psi\rangle$.

concepts.name: Variance
concepts.meaning: The mean squared distance of measurement results from their average.
concepts.formal: $(\Delta A)^2=\langle(A-\langle A\rangle I)^2\rangle=\langle A^2\rangle-\langle A\rangle^2$.
concepts.example: Equal outcomes 2 and 4 have mean 3 and variance 1.

check.prompt: The variance of equally likely 2 and 4 is…
check.explanation: Each squared deviation from 3 equals 1.

concepts.linkedFormal: $(\Delta A)^2=\langle(A-\langle A\rangle I)^2\rangle=\langle A^2\rangle-\langle A\rangle^2$.

concepts.name: Standard Deviation
concepts.meaning: The nonnegative square root of the variance.
concepts.formal: $\Delta A=\sqrt{\langle A^2\rangle-\langle A\rangle^2}$. It is the uncertainty used in the quantum uncertainty relation.

check.prompt: If variance is 4, uncertainty ΔA is…
check.explanation: Take the nonnegative square root.

concepts.linkedFormal: $\Delta A=\sqrt{\langle A^2\rangle-\langle A\rangle^2}$. It is the uncertainty used in the quantum [[Uncertainty Relation|uncertainty relation]].

concepts.name: Schwarz Inequality
concepts.meaning: The overlap of two vectors cannot exceed the product of their lengths.
concepts.formal: $|\langle u|v\rangle|^2\le\langle u|u\rangle\langle v|v\rangle$. Equality holds exactly for linearly dependent vectors, including the zero-vector cases.

check.prompt: For unit vectors, the overlap magnitude is at most…
check.explanation: Both self-inner-products are 1.

concepts.linkedFormal: $|\langle u|v\rangle|^2\le\langle u|u\rangle\langle v|v\rangle$. Equality holds exactly for [[Linear Independence|linearly dependent]] [[Vector|vectors]], including the zero-[[Vector|vector]] cases.

concepts.name: Covariance
concepts.meaning: The symmetric average of two centered observables multiplied together.
concepts.formal: With $A\prime=A-\langle A\rangle I$ and $B\prime=B-\langle B\rangle I$, $\operatorname{Cov}(A,B)=\tfrac12\langle\{A\prime,B\prime\}\rangle$.
concepts.example: If $A=B$, covariance equals the variance of $A$.

check.explanation: The centered product becomes the centered square.

concepts.linkedFormal: With $A\prime=A-\langle A\rangle I$ and $B\prime=B-\langle B\rangle I$, $\operatorname{Cov}(A,B)=\tfrac12\langle\{A\prime,B\prime\}\rangle$.

concepts.name: Uncertainty Relation
concepts.meaning: A lower bound on the product of two measurement spreads.
concepts.formal: For suitable states and Hermitian operators with the required products defined, $\Delta A\Delta B\ge\tfrac12|\langle[A,B]\rangle|$. This is the Robertson bound.
concepts.example: Noncommuting operators can constrain how small both spreads are.

check.explanation: The expected commutator sets this bound.

concepts.linkedFormal: For suitable states and [[Hermitian Operator|Hermitian]] operators with the required products defined, $\Delta A\Delta B\ge\tfrac12|\langle[A,B]\rangle|$. This is the Robertson bound.

concepts.name: Robertson–Schrödinger Relation
concepts.meaning: A stronger uncertainty bound that also includes symmetric correlation.
concepts.formal: $(\Delta A)^2(\Delta B)^2\ge\tfrac14|\langle[A,B]\rangle|^2+\operatorname{Cov}(A,B)^2$. Dropping the nonnegative covariance term gives the Robertson bound.
concepts.example: A nonzero covariance strengthens the lower bound.

check.prompt: Which extra term strengthens the Robertson bound?
check.explanation: The symmetric correlation contributes a nonnegative square.

concepts.linkedFormal: $(\Delta A)^2(\Delta B)^2\ge\tfrac14|\langle[A,B]\rangle|^2+\operatorname{Cov}(A,B)^2$. Dropping the nonnegative [[Covariance|covariance]] term gives the Robertson bound.

concepts.name: Heisenberg Uncertainty Principle
concepts.meaning: Position and momentum spreads cannot both be arbitrarily small.
concepts.formal: Using $[x,p]=i\hbar I$ gives $\Delta x\Delta p\ge\hbar/2$ for normalized states with finite variances and suitable domains.
concepts.example: Halving a minimum-width position spread requires at least doubling the corresponding minimum momentum spread.

check.explanation: Insert the canonical commutator into Robertson.

concepts.linkedFormal: Using $[x,p]=i\hbar I$ gives $\Delta x\Delta p\ge\hbar/2$ for [[Normalization|normalized]] states with finite variances and suitable domains.

concepts.name: Polynomial
concepts.meaning: A finite sum of nonnegative integer powers with numerical coefficients.
concepts.formal: $f(x)=\sum_{k=0}^n c_kx^k$, where $n$ is a nonnegative integer and each $c_k$ is a scalar.

check.explanation: The exponents are nonnegative integers.

concepts.linkedFormal: $f(x)=\sum_{k=0}^n c_kx^k$, where $n$ is a nonnegative [[Integer|integer]] and each $c_k$ is a [[Scalar|scalar]].

concepts.name: Fundamental Theorem of Algebra
concepts.meaning: Every nonconstant polynomial with complex coefficients has a complex root.
concepts.formal: If $p(z)$ is a nonconstant complex polynomial, there exists a complex number $\lambda$ with $p(\lambda)=0$. A degree-n polynomial has n roots counted with their repeated occurrences.

check.prompt: Over the complex numbers, a nonconstant polynomial…
check.explanation: This guarantees a finite complex matrix has an eigenvalue.

concepts.linkedFormal: If $p(z)$ is a nonconstant complex [[Polynomial|polynomial]], there exists a [[Complex Number Arithmetic|complex number]] $\lambda$ with $p(\lambda)=0$. A degree-n [[Polynomial|polynomial]] has n [[Polynomial Root|roots]] counted with their repeated occurrences.

concepts.name: Mathematical Induction
concepts.meaning: A proof that starts with one case and shows how to pass to the next.
concepts.formal: Prove a statement for $n=1$, then prove that its truth for $n$ implies its truth for $n+1$. It then holds for all positive integers.
concepts.example: The finite spectral-theorem proof reduces dimension until the one-dimensional case.

options: A base case and an implication to the next case
check.explanation: Both steps are essential.

concepts.linkedFormal: Prove a statement for $n=1$, then prove that its truth for $n$ implies its truth for $n+1$. It then holds for all positive integers.

concepts.name: Orthogonal Complement
concepts.meaning: All vectors perpendicular to every vector in a chosen subspace.
concepts.formal: $W^\perp=\{v:\langle w|v\rangle=0\text{ for every }w\in W\}$.
concepts.example: The orthogonal complement of the horizontal line in $\mathbb R^2$ is the vertical line.

check.prompt: What complements the span of (1,0) in ℝ²?
check.explanation: Require zero inner product with (1,0).

concepts.linkedFormal: $W^\perp=\{v:\langle w|v\rangle=0\text{ for every }w\in W\}$.

concepts.name: Eigenspace
concepts.meaning: All vectors having a chosen eigenvalue, with the zero vector included.
concepts.formal: The eigenspace for $\lambda$ is $E_\lambda=\{v:Av=\lambda v\}$. It is a vector space; its nonzero members are eigenvectors.

check.explanation: The subspace includes zero although an eigenvector must be nonzero.

concepts.linkedFormal: The eigenspace for $\lambda$ is $E_\lambda=\{v:Av=\lambda v\}$. It is a [[Vector Space|vector space]]; its nonzero members are [[Eigenvector|eigenvectors]].

concepts.name: Associativity
concepts.meaning: Grouping three additions or multiplications does not change the result.
concepts.formal: An operation is associative if $(a+b)+c=a+(b+c)$; for multiplication, $(ab)c=a(bc)$.

check.explanation: Parentheses change but the order stays fixed.

concepts.linkedFormal: An operation is associative if $(a+b)+c=a+(b+c)$; for multiplication, $(ab)c=a(bc)$.

concepts.name: Commutativity
concepts.meaning: Swapping the order of two inputs leaves an operation unchanged.
concepts.formal: Addition is commutative when $a+b=b+a$; multiplication is commutative when $ab=ba$. Matrix multiplication need not be commutative.

check.explanation: Swapping two inputs is the defining test.

concepts.linkedFormal: [[Basic Algebra|Addition]] is commutative when $a+b=b+a$; multiplication is commutative when $ab=ba$. [[Matrix|Matrix]] multiplication need not be commutative.

concepts.name: Distributivity
concepts.meaning: Multiplication spreads across a sum.
concepts.formal: $a(b+c)=ab+ac$. Vector-space scalar multiplication obeys $a(u+v)=au+av$ and $(a+b)v=av+bv$.

check.explanation: Multiply both summands.

concepts.linkedFormal: $a(b+c)=ab+ac$. [[Vector|Vector]]-[[Mathematical Space|space]] [[Scalar|scalar multiplication]] obeys $a(u+v)=au+av$ and $(a+b)v=av+bv$.

concepts.name: Positive Definiteness
concepts.meaning: A rule assigns a positive self-value to every nonzero vector.
concepts.formal: A pairing is positive definite when its self-value is real and positive for each nonzero vector, and is zero for the zero vector.
concepts.example: The sum $|v_1|^2+|v_2|^2$ is positive unless both entries vanish.

check.prompt: A nonzero vector has which self-value in a positive-definite pairing?
check.explanation: Only the zero vector may have self-value zero.

concepts.linkedFormal: A pairing is positive definite when its self-value is real and positive for each nonzero [[Vector|vector]], and is zero for the [[Zero Vector|zero vector]].

concepts.name: Transpose
concepts.meaning: Swap the rows and columns of a matrix.
concepts.formal: $(A^T)_{ij}=A_{ji}$. Transposition alone does not complex-conjugate entries.

check.explanation: Conjugation is a separate operation.

concepts.linkedFormal: $(A^T)_{ij}=A_{ji}$. Transposition alone does not complex-conjugate entries.

concepts.name: Inverse Matrix
concepts.meaning: A matrix that reverses another matrix’s action.
concepts.formal: For a square matrix, $A^{-1}A=AA^{-1}=I$. An inverse exists exactly when the determinant is nonzero.

check.explanation: Composing an action with its inverse returns the input.

concepts.linkedFormal: For a square [[Matrix|matrix]], $A^{-1}A=AA^{-1}=I$. An inverse exists exactly when the [[Determinant|determinant]] is nonzero.

concepts.name: Diagonal Matrix
concepts.meaning: A square matrix whose entries outside the main diagonal are zero.
concepts.formal: $D_{ij}=0$ whenever $i\ne j$; its diagonal entries are $D_{ii}$.

check.prompt: Which entries must vanish in a diagonal matrix?
check.explanation: Only the main diagonal can carry nonzero numbers.

concepts.linkedFormal: $D_{ij}=0$ whenever $i\ne j$; its diagonal entries are $D_{ii}$.

concepts.name: Polynomial Root
concepts.meaning: An input making a polynomial’s output zero.
concepts.formal: $\lambda$ is a root of $p$ if $p(\lambda)=0$.

check.explanation: Substituting the root makes the output zero.

concepts.linkedFormal: $\lambda$ is a root of $p$ if $p(\lambda)=0$.

concepts.name: Multiplicity
concepts.meaning: The number of times a value appears as a repeated polynomial root.
concepts.formal: Algebraic multiplicity of an eigenvalue is its multiplicity as a root of $\det(A-\lambda I)$. For Hermitian matrices it equals the dimension of the eigenspace.
concepts.example: For $2I$ in two dimensions, $(2-\lambda)^2$ gives multiplicity 2.

check.explanation: Count the repeated factor.

concepts.linkedFormal: Algebraic multiplicity of an [[Eigenvalue|eigenvalue]] is its multiplicity as a [[Polynomial Root|root]] of $\det(A-\lambda I)$. For [[Hermitian Operator|Hermitian]] matrices it equals the [[Dimension|dimension]] of the [[Eigenspace|eigenspace]].

concepts.name: Spectrum
concepts.meaning: The set of values where subtracting that value times identity does not have a suitable inverse.
concepts.formal: For a finite matrix, the spectrum is its set of eigenvalues. In infinite dimensions, the spectrum includes continuous values where the inverse fails to be a bounded operator defined on the whole space; bounded means the output norm is at most a fixed constant times the input norm.
concepts.example: Position on the real line has continuous spectrum, not a discrete normalizable eigenbasis.

check.prompt: In finite dimensions, the spectrum is…
options: The diagonal of every basis representation
check.explanation: In infinite dimensions there can also be continuous parts.

concepts.linkedFormal: For a finite [[Matrix|matrix]], the spectrum is its [[Set|set]] of [[Eigenvalue|eigenvalues]]. In infinite dimensions, the spectrum includes [[Continuity|continuous]] values where the [[Inverse Matrix|inverse]] fails to be a bounded [[Linear Operator|operator]] defined on the whole [[Mathematical Space|space]]; bounded means the output [[Norm|norm]] is at most a fixed constant times the input [[Norm|norm]].

concepts.name: Test Function
concepts.meaning: A smooth input function used to probe a distribution.
concepts.formal: A test function here has derivatives of all orders and vanishes outside some bounded interval. Distributions act on such functions.
concepts.example: A smooth bump that is zero outside $[-1,1]$ is a test function.

check.prompt: A test function used here is…
options: Smooth and zero outside a bounded region
Always a constant on the whole line
check.explanation: These conditions make distributional probing well-defined.

concepts.linkedFormal: A test function here has derivatives of all orders and vanishes outside some bounded interval. Distributions act on such functions.

concepts.name: Compact Support
concepts.meaning: A function is zero beyond a finite region.
concepts.formal: On the real line, a function has compact support when it vanishes outside some closed bounded interval.
concepts.example: A function zero for $|x|>1$ has compact support.

check.prompt: Compact support on the line means…
options: Zero outside some finite closed interval
check.explanation: Its nonzero part fits in a finite region.

concepts.linkedFormal: On the real line, a [[Function|function]] has compact support when it vanishes outside some closed bounded interval.

concepts.name: Generalized State
concepts.meaning: An idealized state symbol interpreted through its action on suitable functions.
concepts.formal: Continuous-basis kets such as $|x\rangle$ or $|p\rangle$ are generalized states. They are described distributionally, and need not belong to the ordinary Hilbert space of normalizable states.
concepts.example: Exact position states obey delta normalization.

check.prompt: An exact position ket is usually…
options: An ordinary unit vector in L²
check.explanation: Its normalization is distributional.

concepts.linkedFormal: [[Continuity|Continuous]]-[[Basis|basis]] kets such as $|x\rangle$ or $|p\rangle$ are generalized states. They are described distributionally, and need not belong to the ordinary [[Hilbert Space|Hilbert space]] of [[Normalization|normalizable]] states.

concepts.name: Probability Amplitude
concepts.meaning: A complex number whose squared magnitude gives a probability or density.

concepts.name: Phase
concepts.meaning: The angle describing the direction of a complex number.
concepts.formal: A nonzero complex number is $z=|z|e^{i\theta}$; $\theta$ is its phase. Multiplying an entire state by $e^{i\theta}$ gives a global phase without changing probabilities; relative phases between coefficients can change interference.
concepts.example: $i$ has phase $\pi/2$ relative to positive real numbers.

concepts.name: Symmetric Operator
concepts.meaning: An operator whose action can move across an inner product on its own domain.
concepts.formal: $\langle u|Av\rangle=\langle Au|v\rangle$ for all $u,v\in D(A)$. For unbounded operators this need not imply $D(A)=D(A^\dagger)$, so it need not imply self-adjointness.
concepts.example: A derivative can satisfy the symmetry identity on a restricted domain without being self-adjoint.

concepts.meaning: The half-difference between two opposite-order products.

concepts.name: Probability

concepts.name: Continuity
concepts.meaning: Small input changes near a point produce arbitrarily small output changes.

concepts.name: Normed Space

questions.text: Define a linear vector space and list any three properties that its vectors must satisfy.
questions.answer:
A vector space $V$ over a field $F$ is a set equipped with vector addition and scalar multiplication, satisfying the vector-space axioms.

Closure means $u+v\in V$ and $au\in V$ for $u,v\in V$ and $a\in F$.

1.
A position wave function must have finite $\int|\psi(x)|^2dx$ so a nonzero state can be normalized to total probability 1.

Square-integrable functions, identifying functions equal except on sets of zero length, form a vector space.

This space $L^2$ is complete under its induced norm, so it is a Hilbert space.

Idealized plane waves are generalized states rather than normalizable members of $L^2$.

questions.text: Show that the function ψ(x) = A e⁻ᵃ|ˣ|, a > 0, is square-integrable. Find the normalization constant A.
questions.answer:
1. Taking the absolute-value square gives $|\psi(x)|^2=|A|^2e^{-2a|x|}$.

2. The integrand is even, so $\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}|\psi(x)|^2\,dx=2|A|^2\int_0^{\infty}e^{-2ax}\,dx$.

4. Normalization requires $|A|^2/a=1$. Hence $|A|=\sqrt a$; choosing real positive $A$ gives $A=\sqrt a$. More generally $A=\sqrt a\,e^{i\theta}$, since a global phase does not change probabilities.

questions.title: General uncertainty bound
questions.text: Derive the general uncertainty relation ΔÂ ΔB̂ ≥ ½ |⟨[Â, B̂]⟩|.
questions.answer:
1. For normalized $|\psi\rangle$, let $A'=A-\langle A\rangle I$, $B'=B-\langle B\rangle I$, $|\alpha\rangle=A'|\psi\rangle$, and $|\beta\rangle=B'|\psi\rangle$. Here $\langle A\rangle=\langle\psi|A|\psi\rangle$. Hermiticity gives $\langle\alpha|\alpha\rangle=\langle A^2\rangle-\langle A\rangle^2=(\Delta A)^2$, and similarly for $B$. 4. Taking nonnegative square roots yields $\Delta A\,\Delta B\ge\tfrac12|\langle[A,B]\rangle|$.

questions.title: Real eigenvalues
questions.text: Prove that the eigenvalues of a Hermitian operator are real.
questions.answer:
1. Let $A|v\rangle=\lambda|v\rangle$ with $v\ne0$. Taking the inner product with $v$ gives $\langle v|Av\rangle=\lambda\langle v|v\rangle$.

2. Hermiticity gives $\langle v|Av\rangle=\langle Av|v\rangle=\lambda^*\langle v|v\rangle$, because the first inner-product slot conjugates its scalar coefficient.

3. Therefore $(\lambda-\lambda^*)\langle v|v\rangle=0$. The nonzero eigenvector has strictly positive squared norm, so it can be cancelled and $\lambda=\lambda^*$.

4. A complex number equal to its complex conjugate has zero imaginary part. Hence every eigenvalue of the Hermitian operator is real.

questions.title: Changing a basis
questions.text: Show how an operator transforms under a change of basis.
questions.answer:
1. Let $\{|i\rangle\}$ and $\{|e_j\rangle\}$ be the old and new orthonormal bases. Define $U_{ij}=\langle i|e_j\rangle$, so $|e_j\rangle=\sum_iU_{ij}|i\rangle$. Orthonormality gives $(U^\dagger U)_{mn}=\sum_iU_{im}^*U_{in}=\delta_{mn}$, so $U$ is unitary.

2. Expand both basis vectors: $A'_{mn}=\langle e_m|A|e_n\rangle=\sum_{ij}U_{im}^*\langle i|A|j\rangle U_{jn}=\sum_{ij}U_{im}^*A_{ij}U_{jn}$. Therefore $A'=U^\dagger AU$, and state coordinates satisfy $c'=U^\dagger c$.

3. For a general invertible change-of-basis matrix $S$, whose columns need not be orthonormal, use $A'=S^{-1}AS$ and $c'=S^{-1}c$.

questions.title: Three Hermitian theorems
questions.text:
Hermitian operators represent physical observables in quantum mechanics.
Formulate and prove the three major theorems concerning Hermitian operators:
• Theorem 1: The eigenvalues of a Hermitian operator are strictly real.
• Theorem 2: The eigenvectors of a Hermitian operator corresponding to distinct eigenvalues are mutually orthogonal.
• Theorem 3: The eigenvectors of a Hermitian operator form a complete orthonormal basis for the vector space.
questions.answer:
Assume a finite-dimensional complex inner-product space of dimension $n$. Infinite-dimensional Hermitian or self-adjoint operators need not have a discrete complete eigenbasis; the third theorem requires this finite-dimensional qualification.

(a) Real eigenvalues. Let $Av=\lambda v$, $v\ne0$. Hermiticity gives $\lambda\langle v|v\rangle=\langle v|Av\rangle=\langle Av|v\rangle=\lambda^*\langle v|v\rangle$. Since $\langle v|v\rangle>0$, $\lambda=\lambda^*$, so $\lambda$ is real.

(b) Orthogonality. Let $Au=au$ and $Av=bv$ with distinct real $a,b$. Then $b\langle u|v\rangle=\langle u|Av\rangle=\langle Au|v\rangle=a\langle u|v\rangle$. Since $a\ne b$, the overlap is zero: $\langle u|v\rangle=0$.

questions.title: From Schwarz to Heisenberg
questions.text:
• Starting from the Schwarz inequality for two state vectors |α⟩ = (Â − ⟨Â⟩)|ψ⟩ and |β⟩ = (B̂ − ⟨B̂⟩)|ψ⟩, derive the generalized Robertson-Schrödinger uncertainty relation for any two Hermitian operators Â and B̂: ΔÂ ΔB̂ ≥ ½ |⟨[Â, B̂]⟩|
• Apply this general relation to position x̂ and momentum p̂ₓ to obtain the classic Heisenberg Uncertainty Principle Δx̂ Δp̂ₓ ≥ ℏ/2
questions.answer:
(a) Center the observables. For normalized $|\psi\rangle$, let $A'=A-\langle A\rangle I$, $B'=B-\langle B\rangle I$, $|\alpha\rangle=A'|\psi\rangle$, and $|\beta\rangle=B'|\psi\rangle$. Assume the needed operator products and finite variances exist.

(b) Schwarz gives $(\Delta A)^2(\Delta B)^2\ge|\langle A'B'\rangle|^2$, because $\langle\alpha|\alpha\rangle=\langle(A')^2\rangle=\langle A^2\rangle-\langle A\rangle^2=(\Delta A)^2$ and similarly for $B$.

(c) Decompose $A'B'=\tfrac12\{A',B'\}+\tfrac12[A,B]$. The first expectation is real and the second purely imaginary, since $[A,B]^\dagger=-[A,B]$.

Define $\operatorname{Cov}(A,B)=\tfrac12\langle\{A',B'\}\rangle=\tfrac12\langle AB+BA\rangle-\langle A\rangle\langle B\rangle$. Hence the full Robertson–Schrödinger relation is $(\Delta A)^2(\Delta B)^2\ge\operatorname{Cov}(A,B)^2+\tfrac14|\langle[A,B]\rangle|^2$. Dropping the nonnegative covariance square yields the printed weaker Robertson bound $\Delta A\,\Delta B\ge\tfrac12|\langle[A,B]\rangle|$.

(d) Apply to position and momentum. On a common domain where $[\hat x,\hat p_x]=i\hbar I$, the expectation is $\langle[\hat x,\hat p_x]\rangle=i\hbar\langle\psi|\psi\rangle=i\hbar$.

Therefore $\Delta x\,\Delta p_x\ge\hbar/2$, the Heisenberg uncertainty principle. These spreads are standard deviations over repeated preparations, with finite variances assumed.

questions.text:
• Explain how a state vector |ψ⟩ is represented as a column matrix and an operator Â is represented as a square matrix in a discrete orthonormal basis {|ϕₙ⟩}.
• Formulate the matrix eigenvalue problem Â |ψ⟩ = λ|ψ⟩ as a secular equation det(A − λ I) = 0
• Demonstrate how a unitary transformation Û diagonalizes a Hermitian matrix representation.
• Prove that the trace and eigenvalues of an operator are invariant under unitary transformations.
questions.answer:
Assume finite dimension $n$, so ordinary determinants and traces apply. (a) State representation: $|\psi\rangle=\sum_{j=1}^nc_j|\phi_j\rangle$ with $c_j=\langle\phi_j|\psi\rangle$. Thus the state is the column $\begin{pmatrix}c_1\\\vdots\\c_n\end{pmatrix}$.

The operator entries are $A_{ij}=\langle\phi_i|A|\phi_j\rangle$. Expanding $A|\psi\rangle$ shows that its coefficients are $d_i=\sum_jA_{ij}c_j$, so the operator sends $c$ to $Ac$.

(b) The eigenvalue equation $Ac=\lambda c$ becomes $(A-\lambda I)c=0$. A nonzero solution exists exactly when this square matrix is singular, equivalently $\det(A-\lambda I)=0$. This is the secular equation.

(c) By the finite spectral theorem a Hermitian matrix has an orthonormal eigenbasis $u_1,\ldots,u_n$. Put these vectors into the columns of $U$; orthonormality gives $U^\dagger U=UU^\dagger=I$.

Since $Au_j=\lambda_j u_j$, $AU=UD$ where $D=\operatorname{diag}(\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_n)$. Multiplying by $U^\dagger$ gives $U^\dagger AU=D$, proving unitary diagonalization.

(d) Trace invariance follows from cyclicity: $\operatorname{tr}(U^\dagger AU)=\operatorname{tr}(AUU^\dagger)=\operatorname{tr}A$.

(e) If $Av=\lambda v$, then $(U^\dagger AU)(U^\dagger v)=U^\dagger Av=\lambda U^\dagger v$. Invertibility makes $U^\dagger v\ne0$; the inverse map gives the converse. Also $\det(U^\dagger AU-\lambda I)=\det(U^\dagger)\det(A-\lambda I)\det(U)=\det(A-\lambda I)$. Thus all eigenvalues and their multiplicities are preserved.
